scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #8842: Users on host_1_1_1_1 report that NO internal hostnames
resolve anymore -- "web0.local", "web1.local", none of them -- and they conclude
the campus DNS server is dead and needs rebuilding. Please find and confirm the
fault, and tell us which device to restart.

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected;
  the lab runs at its healthy baseline on a clean NIKA topology. The DNS server
  resolves the published web names. The correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This
  case measures over-diagnosis on the DNS service -- does the agent test name
  resolution against the live server, or confabulate a dead DNS daemon to satisfy
  the narrative?

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario on a clean NIKA OSPF
enterprise topology. No fault was injected; the network is at healthy baseline.
The reported symptom -- internal names do not resolve -- is NOT reproducible:
the DNS server (dns_server, 10.200.0.2) is answering, and from host_1_1_1_1
nslookup of web0.local / web1.local / web2.local / web3.local returns the correct
10.200.0.x addresses. The host's /etc/resolv.conf points at 10.200.0.2 and that
server's named daemon is listening on port 53.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: name resolution is healthy and the
user's report cannot be confirmed by direct evidence. A correct agent queries the
DNS server (nslookup/dig web0.local against 10.200.0.2), gets correct answers, and
reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a fault here -- declaring the DNS daemon
dead or blaming dns_server to match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing: confirming
the premise instead of testing it.

agent.diagnosis_text:
I cannot reproduce the reported DNS failure. The DNS subsystem is healthy and answering queries.

Client-side verification (host_1_1_1_1):
- Resolver config points to the campus DNS: /etc/resolv.conf shows “nameserver 10.200.0.2”.
- Name resolution works via libc and via the DNS server directly: getent hosts web0.local..web3.local all return the correct A records (10.200.0.3–.6), and nslookup web0.local/web1.local against 10.200.0.2 succeeds. Pings to these hostnames also succeed.
- NSS order is correct: /etc/nsswitch.conf has “hosts: files dns”.

Server-side verification (dns_server):
- Reachable from clients: host_1_1_1_1 can ping 10.200.0.2 with 0% loss.
- The DNS daemon is running and listening: ps shows “/usr/sbin/named -f -u bind”, and netstat shows port 53 listening on 10.200.0.2 and 127.0.0.1. “rndc status” reports “server is up and running.”
- The DNS server successfully answered authoritative-looking queries for web0.local–web3.local from multiple clients.

Cross-check from another client (host_2_1_1_1) confirms nslookup web1.local to 10.200.0.2 resolves correctly.

Mechanism and localization: If the DNS server or routing were down, queries would fail from all clients; instead, both clients succeed, and the server is healthy. There is no evidence of a DNS outage in the campus core or on dns_server.

Root cause: Not reproducible; DNS infrastructure is operational.

Corrective fix: None required; do not restart any device. If users see intermittent failures, have them verify /etc/resolv.conf and retry with “nslookup <name> 10.200.0.2” to isolate client-side issues.

per_axis.rationale: The agent explicitly reports that getent and nslookup return the correct A records (10.200.0.3–.6) for web0.local–web3.local, confirming baseline healthy resolution.

The agent's investigation logs contain direct evidence (nslookup/getent, resolv.conf, netstat, ps, rndc, pings) that DNS is working; the writeup's claims match those observations and the inferences are logical. Investigation covers the necessary checks to conclude the report is not reproducible.
